responses: After hearing the arguments from my colleagues, I have shifted my stance to support a **40% allocation to Education**, **20% to Economic Development**, and **20% each to Healthcare and Green Spaces**, with **0% to Infrastructure**. While I initially prioritized infrastructure to fix our crumbling roads, the data regarding teacher turnover and student test scores, combined with the neighbor's success story, convinced me that our immediate human capital is our most critical asset. By investing heavily in education and economic development, we can retain our workforce and attract new families, while the Green Spaces and Healthcare allocations address the quality of life issues that are currently driving people away. I believe this balanced approach tackles the root causes of our community's decline rather than just patching the symptoms.

I would recommend a 30% allocation to Education, 20% to Infrastructure, 20% to Economic Development, 15% to Healthcare, and 15% to Green Spaces, arguing that while the dip in test scores and teacher turnover are concerning, they are symptoms of a larger systemic issue; therefore, we must prioritize Education to stabilize our future workforce, while simultaneously investing in Infrastructure and Economic Development to create the jobs and connectivity that will sustain the community long-term.

I think we need to be realistic about what’s holding this town back; while I love the idea of more parks and better roads, the data shows our schools are the real engine of our future, and if we don't fix the dip in test scores and the teacher turnover, we’re going to lose families to the suburbs. I’m leaning heavily toward a massive investment in Education—maybe 40% of the pot—because if we don't secure our workforce and our next generation, the economic development and infrastructure projects won't matter as much. I’m willing to compromise on the other four areas, but I feel like we have to treat the schools as a crisis priority to stop the brain drain before it gets worse.
